name: GHB
summary: The narrowest margin in this library, for a reason that is entirely kinetic. GHB saturates its own metabolism like alcohol does, so clearance cannot keep up as the dose rises — but its half-life is under an hour, so the dose-response curve is extraordinarily steep in both directions. A small increase in amount produces a disproportionate increase in effect, and the gap between a recreational dose and unconsciousness can be a fraction of a millilitre.
mechanism: An agonist at GABA-B receptors and at its own GHB receptor; it also occurs naturally in the brain in trace amounts. The GABA-B action is responsible for the sedation and for the characteristic abrupt loss of consciousness, which resembles sleep but is not.
elimination_note: Michaelis-Menten, like alcohol: the enzyme saturates at ordinary doses so elimination runs near its maximum of roughly 30 mg/L per hour and the level comes down in close to a straight line. The practical consequence is that doubling the dose much more than doubles the time unconscious, and no amount of waiting shortens it. Note too that the time to peak is not fixed: a larger dose peaks later as well as higher.

oral.note: Rapid absorption, with onset in 15-30 minutes. Food substantially delays and reduces absorption, which is a common cause of accidental redosing — nothing happens, another dose is taken, then both arrive together.

metabolism.primary_enzyme: GHB dehydrogenase, then the Krebs cycle

pathways.name: Succinic semialdehyde
pathways.note: Oxidised and fed into the Krebs cycle, ultimately leaving as carbon dioxide and water. Because it is metabolised to ordinary metabolic products, GHB is almost undetectable within about 6-12 hours — which is why it is so rarely confirmed in suspected drug-facilitated assault.

risk: The distance between the effect people want and unconsciousness is roughly a factor of two in dose. There is no other drug here with so little room, and household measuring is not accurate enough to stay inside it.
Concentration varies enormously between batches of an unregulated liquid, so a volume that was right last time can be twice the dose this time.
With alcohol, the two saturate overlapping metabolic routes and both suppress breathing. This combination accounts for a large share of GHB deaths. See interactions.

Someone unconscious on GHB is not asleep: they can vomit and have no gag reflex. The recovery position and staying with them is the whole intervention, and GHB-related deaths are frequently aspiration rather than respiratory arrest.
Naloxone does not work — this is not an opioid. There is no antidote; it is airway management and time.
Daily use produces physical dependence quickly, and GHB withdrawal is a medical emergency comparable to severe alcohol withdrawal, with delirium and seizures.

sources.text: Brenneisen R et al. Pharmacokinetics and excretion of GHB in healthy subjects. J Anal Toxicol. 2004;28(8):625-30.

uncertainty: Reported GHB concentrations vary by around twofold between studies, because bioavailability estimates range from 25% to 65% and the kinetics are dose-dependent. The absolute numbers here should be treated as indicative. The shape — saturated elimination, a near-linear decline, and a duration that grows disproportionately with dose — is robust across all of them, and it is the shape that carries the risk.
